title: Ch-V-R
hookLine: chaver, chavruta: friend, study partner, joining

cards: The sound reaches you first: a big room full of voices, and nobody quiet. People sit in pairs over open books, reading a line out loud, pointing, arguing, asking each other what it means and then asking again.
Nobody is lecturing. Somebody laughs; somebody slaps the table. In a traditional study hall, this is what learning can sound like.
Each pair is a chavruta. Each partner is a chaver. Today's root is the one that ties them together.

teach.b: Ch-V-R. Chet, vet, resh. To join, to connect.
A chaver is a friend, a companion; a chavruta, a study partnership. First, joining. When the tabernacle is built, its curtains are "coupled together one to another," and the Hebrew uses this root.
A psalm calls Jerusalem "a city that is compact together," joined to itself: the same letters again. A friend, in this root, is someone you're fastened to. Second, choosing.
The sayings of the fathers teach: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend. A teacher you appoint. A friend, the Hebrew says, you acquire, as if it costs you something.
The Talmud tells of Choni, who slept for seventy years. He wakes and goes to the study hall, and hears the scholars saying how clear the teaching used to be in Choni's day. He tells them who he is.
They don't believe him, and don't give him the honor due. Heartbroken, he prays for mercy and dies. And the sage Rava says: this is why people say, o chavruta o mituta.
Either companionship, or death. Fourth, the pair. That's the weight a study partner carries.
Your chaver catches what you missed, pushes back, asks the question you were avoiding. In this root, a friend isn't a spectator to your life.

teach.h: A FRIEND IS JOINED TO THE WORK.
teach.b: A friend is joined to the work.

how: In a traditional beit midrash, students learn in chavruta, pairs who read the text aloud and question each other; Pirkei Avot teaches 'acquire for yourself a friend', and the Talmud's saying 'either companionship or death' comes from the story of Choni.

o: the Hebrew root of debt and owing
the Hebrew root of choosing, the chosen one
the Hebrew root of joining, friend and partner

s: a chavruta studies in silence, alone
a chavruta is a pair, reading aloud and questioning each other.
the sayings of the fathers teach to acquire a friend
make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend.
when Choni woke, the scholars welcomed him
they didn't believe him. Rava: either companionship, or death.

games.q: you're Choni. you wake after seventy years, and the study hall won't believe who you are. what happens?
o: you start over with new friends.
heartbroken, you pray for mercy and die.
games.why: the Talmud says he prayed and died, and Rava said: o chavruta o mituta, either companionship or death.

practice: Bring one friend to mind, someone you'd call if something went wrong, or someone you've drifted from, and remember one thing you know because of them: a skill, a habit, a way of seeing.
Then think of one small way to join them, a call, a walk, a page you could read together, and if you pray, pray for them by name.
If loneliness ever feels too heavy to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Ch-V-R. Chet, vet, resh: chaver, a friend, and chavruta, a study pair. To be joined. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic: a study partnership, from chet, vet, resh, the root of chaver, friend.

carryVoice: Your line: friendship joins. A friend, in Hebrew, is someone you're fastened to. Until tomorrow.
